notes.meaning: Saul returned from fighting the Philistines and immediately learned that David was hiding in the wilderness near En-gedi. En-gedi was an oasis along the cliffs of the Dead Sea, full of deep limestone caves. Saul was so determined to destroy David that he resumed his hunt without taking any rest.

Saul gathered three thousand of his best soldiers from all Israel to hunt David and his small band. The "Rocks of the Wild Goats" was a rugged, dangerous area where only mountain goats could easily climb. Bringing such a massive force showed that Saul viewed David as a major rival rather than a harmless fugitive.

Saul came upon stone sheepfolds near the road and entered a large cave to relieve himself. David and his men were already hiding in the dark, deep recesses of that very cave. From the shadows, David's men could clearly see Saul enter, while Saul could not see them at all.

David's men urged him to strike, claiming God had handed his enemy over to him. David crept forward quietly and cut off the corner of Saul's robe without being noticed. He refused to kill Saul, choosing not to use sinful shortcuts to reach the throne God had promised him.

Right after cutting the cloth, David felt deep guilt in his heart. Even though he had spared Saul's life, he felt that damaging the royal garment was an act of disrespect toward the king. His quick remorse shows how sensitive his conscience was toward God.

David told his men that the Lord forbade him from harming Saul. Saul was God's anointed king, chosen and set apart by God's authority, so only God had the right to remove him. David knew that honoring God meant respecting the ruler God had placed over the nation.

other.view: Augustine taught that David respected the enduring sacredness of the anointing itself, which remained holy in Saul even though Saul's personal conduct was wicked.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that this verse forbids ordinary believers from questioning or evaluating church leaders. Many evangelicals answer that the text forbids physical violence and rebellion, not honest accountability or biblical correction.

notes.meaning: David strongly corrected his men and ordered them not to harm Saul. He refused to let his followers carry out a murder that he himself would not commit. Saul then got up, walked out of the cave, and went on his way without realizing what had happened.

David stepped out of the cave and called out after the king. When Saul turned around, David bowed with his face to the earth in deep reverence. This humble posture proved to Saul that David was a loyal subject, not a rebellious enemy trying to seize power.

David asked Saul why he paid attention to people who claimed David wanted to hurt him. Rather than accusing the king directly, David tactfully blamed the slanderers and gossips at court. He urged Saul to look at real evidence instead of trusting malicious rumors.

David told Saul that the Lord had put the king in his power inside the cave that very day. His men had urged him to strike, but David took pity on him and spared him. He reminded Saul that he would never raise his hand against the leader God had anointed.

David held up the piece of cloth and addressed Saul with respect as his father. The cut hem proved that David could have taken Saul's life just as easily, yet chose mercy instead. This physical evidence proved that David had no rebellion or evil intent in his heart.

David asked the Lord to judge between the two of them and decide who was right. If Saul continued to hunt him unjustly, David trusted God to deliver him and bring justice. At the same time, David made it clear that he would never lift his own hand against Saul.

David cited an old proverb that says evil actions come from evil people. If David were truly a wicked traitor, he would have killed Saul when he had the chance. His choice to spare the king proved that his character was not wicked.

David asked why the mighty king of Israel was chasing someone so harmless and weak. He compared himself to a dead dog and a single flea, creatures that pose no danger and have no value. Chasing after such an insignificant target was completely beneath the king's royal dignity.

David repeated that the Lord must be their judge and decide the dispute. He asked God to look upon his hardship, defend his innocent cause, and rescue him from Saul's hand. David was content to wait for God's deliverance rather than avenge himself.

When David finished speaking, Saul recognized his voice and called him his son. Overwhelmed by David's astonishing kindness and his own guilt, Saul wept aloud. David's gentle humility broke through Saul's hard heart and softened his anger for the moment.

Saul openly confessed that David was more righteous than he was. David had repaid cruelty with goodness, while Saul had repaid faithful service with hatred. Even Saul had to admit the undeniable proof of David's upright conduct.

Saul acknowledged how wonderfully David had treated him that day. God had delivered Saul into David's hands, yet David refused to harm him. Saul saw that David had acted with extraordinary mercy toward his pursuer.

Saul remarked that when people corner an enemy, they do not let him walk away unharmed. Because Saul could not properly repay such mercy, he asked the Lord to bless David for what he had done. David's refusal to retaliate turned aside wrath with good.

Saul admitted out loud that David would certainly become king of Israel. God's obvious protection of David and David's noble character convinced Saul that God's plan could never be stopped. This was Saul's first public confession of the truth he had tried so hard to fight against.

Saul asked David to swear an oath before God that he would not wipe out his family once he became king. In the ancient world, new rulers often killed the family of the previous king to stop any future rebellion. Saul knew David kept his promises and would honor an oath made to the Lord.

David gave Saul his solemn oath, and Saul headed back home. David and his men, however, returned to their mountain stronghold instead of going with the king. David knew how quickly Saul's moods could change and wisely chose not to risk his life on a passing emotional apology.
